contents.text: On March 1, 1861, a few months after the Southern states seceded, Abraham Lincoln took the oath of office to become president. The passage below comes from the speech Lincoln gave right after taking the oath of office. In the speech, Lincoln addressed the people of the seceded states. He described to them what he saw as his primary duty as president.
Select the phrase or sentence that states that duty.

text.text: In your hands, my dissatisfied fellow-countrymen, and not in mine, is the momentous issue of civil war.
<atomic>You can have no conflict without being yourselves the aggressors.</atomic>
You have no oath … to destroy the government,

contents.text: Lincoln said that he had made an important promise to "preserve, protect, and defend" the United States. He implied that he would not let the Southern states break away from the United States.
In the rest of the passage, Lincoln uses the word "you" to show that he is talking about the responsibilities of people in seceded states, not his own role as president.

explanationText.text: Handy said that the Republicans would ban slavery in the District of Columbia. The District of Columbia is another name for Washington, D.C.

Handy said that the Republican Party would "exclude slavery from all the territories." In the 1800s, the federal government controlled a large amount of land that wasn't part of states. Slaveholders wanted to allow slavery in these territories.

explanationText.text: Handy does not mention a law to arm enslaved people.

contents.text: In order to manufacture clothing, the United Kingdom imported a large amount of cotton. Before the Civil War, the United Kingdom imported most of its cotton from the Southern states.

The graph below shows cotton imports for the United Kingdom. The graph's data starts with 1860, the year that Southern states began to secede, and ends with 1864, the last full year of the Civil War. Look at the graph. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A line graph titled "Cotton imports into the United Kingdom, 1860-1864." In 1860, the United Kingdom imported about 400,000 tons of cotton. Almost all of this cotton came from the United States. From 1861-1864, this changed significantly: Imports from the United States fell below 300,000 tons in 1861, below 75,000 tons in 1862, then below 50,000 tons in 1863 and 1864. Meanwhile, imports from other countries were steadily increasing. The United Kingdom imported less than 25,000 tons of cotton from Egypt in 1860, but over 50,000 tons in 1864. The United Kingdom also imported less than 25,000 tons of cotton from India in 1860, which sharply increased to around 130,000 tons in 1861 and continued increasing to over 200,000 tons in 1864.

subpoints.text: Cotton played an important part in the global economy of the 1800s. Plantation owners sent raw cotton to mills in places such as New England and the United Kingdom. These mills would then turn the cotton into clothing and bedding. From shippers to merchants to mill workers, hundreds of thousands of people outside the South depended on cotton to earn their livelihoods.

contents.text: In order to manufacture clothing, the United Kingdom imported a large amount of cotton. Before the Civil War, the United Kingdom imported most of its cotton from the Southern states.

The graph below shows cotton imports for the United Kingdom. The graph's data starts with 1860, the year that Southern states began to secede, and ends with 1864, the last full year of the Civil War. Look at the graph. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A line graph titled "Cotton imports into the United Kingdom, 1860-1864." In 1860, the United Kingdom imported about 400,000 tons of cotton. Almost all of this cotton came from the United States. From 1861-1864, this changed significantly: Imports from the United States fell below 300,000 tons in 1861, below 75,000 tons in 1862, then below 50,000 tons in 1863 and 1864. Meanwhile, imports from other countries were steadily increasing. The United Kingdom imported less than 25,000 tons of cotton from Egypt in 1860, but over 50,000 tons in 1864. The United Kingdom also imported less than 25,000 tons of cotton from India in 1860, which sharply increased to around 130,000 tons in 1861 and continued increasing to over 200,000 tons in 1864.

subheader.text: Why did Confederate soldiers kill African American soldiers at Fort Pillow?

subpoints.text: Most African American soldiers in the Union army were formerly enslaved people. The Confederate government saw these Union soldiers as stolen property. They refused to treat the captured African American people like other prisoners of war.
At Fort Pillow, Confederate soldiers were enraged that formerly enslaved people were fighting against them. Over 300 African American soldiers were killed, most when they tried to surrender.

content.text: Some Southern cities were burned down during the war.

explanationText.text: LeConte describes the city of Columbia as "in ashes" and "in ruins." She uses these words to describe how Columbia looked after it had been burned down by the Union army.

content.text: The Union and Confederate armies stayed far away from Southerners' homes.

explanationText.text: LeConte describes visiting a city that had been burned down. The Union and Confederate armies fought and moved throughout the South, including through areas where many civilians lived.

elements.text: A white Southerner who wanted to elect new leaders would probably support Republican plans to replace Confederate leaders. And a white Southerner who wanted to improve the South would probably support Republican plans to improve education and create new jobs.

elements.text: The Republicans wanted to improve workers' skills and help businesses create new jobs. Those changes would help the African American man. He might go to school to learn new skills, and he might get one of the new, non-farming jobs.

elements.text: The Republicans' plans would give workers more skills and better job opportunities. This could make it harder for the planter to find people to pick his crops. So, he would probably prefer the Democrats, who mostly wanted to leave the South the way it was.

building schools to improve workers' knowledge and skills, so some of them could take non-farming jobs
building railroads to get Southern products to Northern markets
reducing taxes on businesses so they could create new, non-farming jobs

header.text: These choices are correct. These people would be likely to vote for the Republican Party:

content.text: A Northern businessman who wanted to open a factory in the South

explanationText.text: The Republicans wanted to reduce taxes on businesses and build more railroads. Those changes would help the Northern businessman. He could pay lower taxes if he opened a factory in the South, and he could use the new railroads to sell his products in the North.

content.text: A white Southerner who wanted new leaders who would improve the South

explanationText.text: A white Southerner who wanted to elect new leaders would probably support Republican plans to replace Confederate leaders. And a white Southerner who wanted to improve the South would probably support Republican plans to improve education and create new jobs.

content.text: An African American man who wanted to learn new skills to get a better job

explanationText.text: The Republicans wanted to improve workers' skills and help businesses create new jobs. Those changes would help the African American man. He might go to school to learn new skills, and he might get one of the new, non-farming jobs.

be likely to vote for the Republican Party:

content.text: A white planter who relied on low-skilled workers to plant his crops

explanationText.text: The Republicans' plans would give workers more skills and better job opportunities. This could make it harder for the planter to find people to pick his crops. So, he would probably prefer the Democrats, who mostly wanted to leave the South the way it was.

header.text: The passage below comes from an investigation into the murder of an African American man named Johnson Stuart. The man's brother is describing what happened before the murder. Read the passage. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: Question—Did you ever hear of any threats being made against him before he was killed?…
Answer—Major Tom Wadlington told me my brother was marked that day of the Sheriff's election.
Question—Did he say what he meant by marked?

Answer—He said he was marked. I said, "What about? He never did anything." He said, "He stood on the courthouse steps that day." I said, "Well, [the sheriff] told him to stand there to keep back the crowd from crowding up." Major Wadlington said, "Yes, but he kept back the white people too." I said, "No, he let them in in their turn. All went in, and all were treated alike." He said, "Well, he should not have done that way; he ought to have let the white people in."

laws to restrict the rights of African American people. From the late 1800s to the 1960s, these Jim Crow laws limited African American people's rights.

In both the North and South, states passed laws that segregated almost every part of society. The Supreme Court reviewed one Louisiana segregation law in the case
. Read about the case. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: In 1890, Louisiana passed a law segregating train cars. Homer Plessy, a mixed-race Black man, protested the law by boarding a whites-only car in New Orleans. He was arrested but challenged the law in court. His lawyers argued segregated train cars broke the Fourteenth Amendment, which guaranteed all citizens equal protection under the law.

The Supreme Court decided segregation was constitutional because the Fourteenth Amendment did not specifically guarantee social equality. The ruling said states, cities, and private businesses could make public places "separate but equal," meaning segregated. In reality, segregated places were designed to be unequal and to make African American people feel inferior.

In both the North and South, states passed laws that segregated almost every part of society. The Supreme Court reviewed one Louisiana segregation law in the case
. Read about the case. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: In 1890, Louisiana passed a law segregating train cars. Homer Plessy, a mixed-race Black man, protested the law by boarding a whites-only car in New Orleans. He was arrested but challenged the law in court. His lawyers argued segregated train cars broke the Fourteenth Amendment, which guaranteed all citizens equal protection under the law.

The Supreme Court decided segregation was constitutional because the Fourteenth Amendment did not specifically guarantee social equality. The ruling said states, cities, and private businesses could make public places "separate but equal," meaning segregated. In reality, segregated places were designed to be unequal and to make African American people feel inferior.

pieces.text: After the end of the Civil War, the United States outlawed slavery, and Reconstruction began. During Reconstruction, U.S. soldiers remained in the South to enforce new laws that protected African American people's rights. But in 1877, President Hays removed federal troops from the South and Reconstruction ended. With the U.S. soldiers gone, Southern states passed
laws to restrict the rights of African American people. From the late 1800s to the 1960s, these Jim Crow laws limited African American people's rights.

In both the North and South, states passed laws that segregated almost every part of society. The Supreme Court reviewed one Louisiana segregation law in the case
. Read about the case. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: In 1890, Louisiana passed a law segregating train cars. Homer Plessy, a mixed-race Black man, protested the law by boarding a whites-only car in New Orleans. He was arrested but challenged the law in court. His lawyers argued segregated train cars broke the Fourteenth Amendment, which guaranteed all citizens equal protection under the law.

The Supreme Court decided segregation was constitutional because the Fourteenth Amendment did not specifically guarantee social equality. The ruling said states, cities, and private businesses could make public places "separate but equal," meaning segregated. In reality, segregated places were designed to be unequal and to make African American people feel inferior.

pieces.text: After the end of the Civil War, the United States outlawed slavery, and Reconstruction began. During Reconstruction, U.S. soldiers remained in the South to enforce new laws that protected African American people's rights. But in 1877, President Hays removed federal troops from the South and Reconstruction ended. With the U.S. soldiers gone, Southern states passed
laws to restrict the rights of African American people. From the late 1800s to the 1960s, these Jim Crow laws limited African American people's rights.

draggableItems.text: Grandfather clauses: If someone's grandfather was able to vote before 1865, they did not have to pay a poll tax or take a literacy test. Enslaved people were not allowed to vote.

Literacy tests: Many states passed laws that people could not register to vote unless they passed a reading test.

In both the North and South, states passed laws that segregated almost every part of society. The Supreme Court reviewed one Louisiana segregation law in the case
. Read about the case. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: In 1890, Louisiana passed a law segregating train cars. Homer Plessy, a mixed-race Black man, protested the law by boarding a whites-only car in New Orleans. He was arrested but challenged the law in court. His lawyers argued segregated train cars broke the Fourteenth Amendment, which guaranteed all citizens equal protection under the law.

The Supreme Court decided segregation was constitutional because the Fourteenth Amendment did not specifically guarantee social equality. The ruling said states, cities, and private businesses could make public places "separate but equal," meaning segregated. In reality, segregated places were designed to be unequal and to make African American people feel inferior.

pieces.text: After the end of the Civil War, the United States outlawed slavery, and Reconstruction began. During Reconstruction, U.S. soldiers remained in the South to enforce new laws that protected African American people's rights. But in 1877, President Hays removed federal troops from the South and Reconstruction ended. With the U.S. soldiers gone, Southern states passed
laws to restrict the rights of African American people. From the late 1800s to the 1960s, these Jim Crow laws limited African American people's rights.
